implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the hook contract (abstract class, interface or callback signature) that application code implements, and let the framework own the sequence - main loop, lifecycle, request dispatch, executor - calling the hooks through that contract. Register implementations explicitly (subclassing, a registration call, configuration or convention) so the framework can find them, and make the framework's dependencies point only at the contract, never at concrete extensions. Decide and document the calling contract: order, thread, lifecycle guarantees, failure and cancellation semantics, and how registrations are removed.
code_sketch:
framework side: owns the flow and calls the contract
for event in loop():
    for hook in registry.for_type(event.type):
        hook(event)                     # application code runs here

application side: implements and registers, never drives
def handle(event): ...
registry.add(Order.CREATED, handle)
pitfalls: Inverting for one implementation and one call site: the registration and lifecycle machinery costs more than the direct call it replaces.
Leaving the calling contract implicit: undocumented order, thread and failure semantics turn simple hooks into intermittent bugs.
Registrations with no owner and no removal path: hooks outlive their state and touch disposed objects.

Constructor versus setter injection confusion: setter injection (post-construction wiring) makes the object partially-constructed and breaks invariants; prefer constructor injection unless a circular dependency genuinely requires it.

IoC container as a service locator in disguise: passing the container itself into a component (container.resolve<T>()) recreates a static locator and hides the actual dependency graph; the component should declare its dependencies, not fetch them.

Ambient context abuse: thread-local or request-scoped context objects accessed inside a hook make the hook non-deterministic and untestable without the ambient state; inject the context explicitly instead.

Hidden diamond dependency: A depends on B and C, both depend on D but register different concrete subtypes of D; the container resolves one silently, producing a runtime error that surfaces only when the mismatched instance is used.

The myth that IoC always improves testability: a framework-bound hook called through the real dispatch sequence requires the real framework to test; this is harder to set up than a plain unit test, not easier; the testability benefit requires that hooks are thin delegates to plain objects.

Wrong move: inject the IoC container into application hooks and resolve services on demand -> dependency lookup hides required dependencies and recreates a service locator -> instead keep the container at the composition root and inject explicit collaborators.
